parts.text:
Find the first 4 terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of
$$\left(1+\frac{3x}{2}\right)^8$$
giving each term in its simplest form.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $1+12x$ both terms correct as printed (allow $12x^1$ but not $1^8$).
M1: For either the $x^2$ term or the $x^3$ term. Requires correct binomial coefficient in any form with the correct power of $x$, but the other part of the coefficient (perhaps including powers of 2 and/or 3 or signs) may be wrong or missing, e.g. $\left(\frac{8(7)}{2!}\times \ldots \times x^2\right)$ or $\left(\frac{8(7)(6)}{3!}\times \ldots \times x^3\right)$ or $\left(^8C_2\times\ldots\times x^2\right)$ or $\left(^8C_3\times\ldots\times x^3\right)$.
Special Case: Allow this M1 only for an attempt at a descending expansion provided the equivalent conditions are met for any term other than the first.
A1: Either $63x^2$ or $189x^3$.
A1: Both $63x^2$ and $189x^3$.
Terms may be listed but must be positive.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $... + \frac{8(7)}{2!}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{8(7)(6)}{3!}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^3 + ...$ or $... + {}^8C_2\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^2 + {}^8C_3\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^3 + ...$
- e.g. $... + 8\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^7(1) + \frac{8(7)}{2!}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^6(1)^2 + ...$ or $... + {}^8C_1\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^7 + {}^8C_2\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^6 + ...$
- Note it is common not to square the 2 in the denominator of $\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)$ and this gives $1+12x+126x^2+756x^3$. This could score B1M1A0A0.
- Note $... + {}^8C_2\left(1^4+\frac{3x}{2}\right)^2 + {}^8C_3\left(1^3+\frac{3x}{2}\right)^3 + ...$ would score M0 unless a correct method was implied by later work

questions.stem:
A geometric series has first term $a$, where $a \neq 0$, and common ratio $r$.
The sum to infinity of this series is 6 times the first term of the series.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that $r=\frac{5}{6}$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Either $\frac{a}{1-r}=6a$ or $\frac{6a}{1-r}=a$ or $\frac{6}{1-r}=1$.
A1*: cso, $\Rightarrow 1=6(1-r)\Rightarrow r=\frac{5}{6}$. Allow verification e.g. $\frac{a}{1-r}=6a\Rightarrow \frac{a}{1-\frac{5}{6}}=6a\Rightarrow \frac{a}{\frac{1}{6}}=6a\Rightarrow 6a=6a$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that the fourth term of this series is 62.5
(b) find the value of $a$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\{T_4=ar^3=62.5\Rightarrow\} a\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^3=62.5$ (correct statement using the 4th term; do not accept $a\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4=62.5$).
A1: $a=108$.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) find the difference between the sum to infinity and the sum of the first 30 terms, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Correct method to find $S_\infty$: $S_\infty=6(\text{their } a)$ or $\frac{\text{their }a}{1-\frac{5}{6}}\{=648\}$.
M1: $S_{30}=\frac{(\text{their }a)\left(1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{30}\right)}{1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)}$ (condone invisible brackets around 5/6).
A1ft: Correct follow through expression (follow through their $a$); do not condone invisible brackets around 5/6 unless their evaluation or final answer implies they were intended.
A1: $\{S_\infty-S_{30}\}=2.72984\ldots$, awrt 2.73.
Alternative: Difference $=\frac{ar^{30}}{1-r}=\frac{108\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{30}}{1-\frac{5}{6}}=2.72984\ldots$. M1M1: For an attempt to apply $\frac{ar^{30}}{1-r}$. A1ft: $\frac{(\text{their }a)\times r^{30}}{1-r}$ with their ft $a$. A1: awrt 2.73.

Figure 1 shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation $y=\sqrt{(2x-1)}$, $x \geqslant 0.5$

The finite region $R$, shown shaded in Figure 1, is bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines with equations $x=2$ and $x=10$.

The table below shows corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for $y=\sqrt{(2x-1)}$.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 10\\ \hline y & \sqrt{3} & & \sqrt{11} & & \sqrt{19}\\ \hline\end{array}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Complete the table with the values of $y$ corresponding to $x=4$ and $x=8$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Both $\sqrt{7}$ and $\sqrt{15}$. Allow awrt 2.65 and 3.87.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use the trapezium rule, with all the values of $y$ in the completed table, to find an approximate value for the area of $R$, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Outside brackets $\frac{1}{2}\times 2$ or $1$ (may be implied).
M1: For structure of $\{\ldots\}$: Area$(R)\approx \frac{1}{2}\times 2;\times\{\sqrt{3}+2(\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{15})+\sqrt{19}\}$. Requires the correct structure for the $y$ values: contain first $y$ value plus last $y$ value and the second bracket to be multiplied by 2 and to be the summation of the remaining $y$ values in the table with no additional values. If the only mistake is a copying error or omits one value from the $2(\ldots)$ bracket this may be regarded as a slip and the M mark can be allowed (an extra repeated term forfeits the M mark). M0 if any values used are $x$ values instead of $y$ values. Alternative: separate trapezia may be used and marked equivalently, B1 for $\frac{1}{2}\times 2$, M1 for correct structure.
A1: cao, $=25.76$ (2dp).
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Note decimal values are $\frac{1}{2}\times 2;\times\{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{19}+2(\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{15})\}=\frac{1}{2}\times 2;\times\{6.0909..+19.6707...\}$
- Bracketing mistakes: e.g. $\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2\right)\times(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{19})+2(\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{15})$ $\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2\right)\times\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{19}+2(\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{15})$ Both score B1 M1
- $\left[\frac{1}{2}\times 2(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{7})+\frac{1}{2}\times 2(\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{11})+\frac{1}{2}\times 2(\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{15})+\frac{1}{2}\times 2(\sqrt{15}+\sqrt{19})\right]$
- $=1\times 25.76166865... = 25.76166... = 25.76$ (2dp)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) State whether your approximate value in part (b) is an overestimate or an underestimate for the area of $R$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: underestimate. Accept 'under', 'less than' etc.

questions.stem:
$$\mathrm{f}(x)=-4x^3+ax^2+9x-18, \text{ where } a \text{ is a constant.}$$
Given that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $\mathrm{f}(x)$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the value of $a$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts $\mathrm{f}(2)$ or $\mathrm{f}(-2)$: $\mathrm{f}(2)=-32+4a+18-18=0$.
A1: cso, $\Rightarrow 4a=32\Rightarrow a=8$.
Way 2: $\mathrm{f}(x)=(x-2)(px^2+qx+r)=px^3+(q-2p)x^2+(r-2q)x-2r$. M1: Compares coefficients leading to $r=9\Rightarrow q=0$ also $p=-4\therefore a=-2p=8$. A1: cso, $a=8$.
Way 3: $(-4x^3+ax^2+9x-18)\div(x-2)$. M1: Attempt to divide $\pm \mathrm{f}(x)$ by $(x-2)$ to give a quotient at least of the form $\pm 4x^2+g(a)x$ and a remainder that is a function of $a$: $Q=-4x^2+(a-8)x+2a-7$, $R=4a-32$. A1: cso, $4a-32=0\Rightarrow a=8$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) factorise $\mathrm{f}(x)$ completely,
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts long division or other method, to obtain $\mathrm{f}(x)=(x-2)(-4x^2\pm ax\pm b)$, $b\neq 0$, even with a remainder. Working need not be seen as this could be done "by inspection": $\mathrm{f}(x)=(x-2)(-4x^2+9)$.
dM1: A valid attempt to factorise their quadratic (dependent on the previous method mark being awarded, but there must have been no remainder): $=(x-2)(3-2x)(3+2x)$ or equivalent e.g. $=-(x-2)(2x-3)(2x+3)$ or $=(x-2)(2x-3)(-2x-3)$.
A1: cao, must have all 3 factors on the same line. Ignore subsequent work (such as a solution to a quadratic equation).

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) find the remainder when $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is divided by $(2x-1)$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts $\mathrm{f}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ or $\mathrm{f}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)$: $\mathrm{f}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-4\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+8\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+9\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-18=-12$.
A1ft: Allow A1ft for the correct numerical value of $\frac{\text{their }a}{4}-14$.
Way 2: $\pm(-4x^3+8x^2+9x-18)\div(2x-1)$. M1: Attempt long division to give a remainder that is independent of $x$: $Q=-2x^2+3x+6$, $R=-12$. A1ft: Allow A1ft for the correct numerical value of $\frac{\text{their }a}{4}-14$.

questions.stem:
Figure 2 shows the shape $ABCDEA$ which consists of a right-angled triangle $BCD$ joined to a sector $ABDEA$ of a circle with radius 7 cm and centre $B$.

$A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a straight line with $AB=7$ cm.

Given that the size of angle $ABD$ is exactly 2.1 radians,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find, in cm, the length of the arc $DEA$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $7\times 2.1$ only.
A1: Length $DEA=7(2.1)=14.7$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) find, in cm, the perimeter of the shape $ABCDEA$, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Angle $CBD=\pi-2.1$. May be seen on the diagram (allow awrt 1.0 and allow $180-120$). Could score for sight of Angle $CBD=$ awrt 60 degrees.
dM1: A correct attempt to find $BC$ and $BD$ (dependent on the previous method mark): both $7\cos(\pi-2.1)$ and $7\sin(\pi-2.1)$, or both $7\cos(\pi-2.1)$ and $\sqrt{7^2-(7\cos(\pi-2.1))^2}$, or both $7\sin(\pi-2.1)$ and $\sqrt{7^2-(7\sin(\pi-2.1))^2}$ or equivalents to these. $7\cos(\pi-2.1)$ can be implied by awrt 3.5 and $7\sin(\pi-2.1)$ can be implied by awrt 6. If the sine rule is used, do not allow mixing of degrees and radians unless their answer implies a correct interpretation. Note: 2.1 radians is 120 degrees (to 3sf) which if used gives angle $CBD$ as 60 degrees, and if used this gives a correct perimeter of 31.3 and could score full marks.
ddM1: $P=\text{their }BC+\text{their }CD+7+\text{their }DEA$ (dependent on both previous method marks).
A1: $=31.2764\ldots$, awrt 31.3.

questions.stem:
Figure 3 shows a sketch of part of the curve $C$ with equation
$$y=\frac{1}{8}x^3+\frac{3}{4}x^2, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$$

The curve $C$ has a maximum turning point at the point $A$ and a minimum turning point at the origin $O$.

The line $l$ touches the curve $C$ at the point $A$ and cuts the curve $C$ at the point $B$.

The $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $-4$ and the $x$ coordinate of $B$ is 2.

The finite region $R$, shown shaded in Figure 3, is bounded by the curve $C$ and the line $l$.

parts.text:
Use integration to find the area of the finite region $R$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $x^n\to x^{n+1}$ on either term.
A1: $\int\left(\frac{1}{8}x^3+\frac{3}{4}x^2\right)dx=\frac{x^4}{32}+\frac{x^3}{4}\{+c\}$; any correct simplified or un-simplified form (+c not required).
dM1: Substitutes limits of 2 and $-4$ into an "integrated function" and subtracts either way round. Or substitutes limits of 0 and $-4$ and 2 and 0 into an "integrated function" and subtracts either way round and adds the two results.
A1: $=\frac{21}{2}$ or $10.5$. (At $x=-4$, $y=-8+12=4$ or at $x=2$, $y=1+3=4$.)
M1: Area of Rectangle $=6\times 4=24$ or Area of Rectangles $=4\times 4=16$ and $2\times 4=8$. Evidence of $(4--2)\times \text{their }y_{-4}$ or $(4--2)\times\text{their }y_2$, or evidence of $4\times\text{their }y_{-4}$ and $2\times\text{their }y_2$.
dddM1: Area rectangle − integrated answer, dependent on all previous method marks and requires: Rectangle > integration > 0.
A1: So, area$(R)=24-\frac{21}{2}=\frac{27}{2}$ or 13.5.

Figure 4 shows the plan of a pool.

The shape of the pool $ABCDEFA$ consists of a rectangle $BCEF$ joined to an equilateral triangle $BFA$ and a semi-circle $CDE$, as shown in Figure 4.

Given that $AB=x$ metres, $EF=y$ metres, and the area of the pool is 50 m$^2$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that
$$y=\frac{50}{x}-\frac{x}{8}(\pi+2\sqrt{3})$$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: An attempt to find 3 areas of the form: $xy$, $p\pi x^2$ and $qx^2$.
A1: Correct expression for $A$ (terms must be added): $\{A=\}xy+\frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60°$.
A1*: $50=xy+\frac{\pi x^2}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}\Rightarrow y=\frac{50}{x}-\frac{\pi x}{8}-\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{4}\Rightarrow y=\frac{50}{x}-\frac{x}{8}(\pi+2\sqrt{3})$. Correct proof with no errors seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence show that the perimeter, $P$ metres, of the pool is given by
$$P=\frac{100}{x}+\frac{x}{4}(\pi+8-2\sqrt{3})$$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Correct expression for $P$ in terms of $x$ and $y$: $\{P=\}\frac{\pi x}{2}+2x+2y$.
M1: Substitutes the given expression for $y$ into an expression for $P$ where $P$ is at least of the form $\alpha x+\beta y$: $P=\frac{\pi x}{2}+2x+2\left(\frac{50}{x}-\frac{x}{8}(\pi+2\sqrt{3})\right)$.
$P=\frac{\pi x}{2}+2x+\frac{100}{x}-\frac{\pi x}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}x\Rightarrow P=\frac{100}{x}+\frac{\pi x}{4}+2x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}x$.
A1*: $\Rightarrow P=\frac{100}{x}+\frac{x}{4}(\pi+8-2\sqrt{3})$. Correct proof with no errors seen. (Note $\frac{\pi+8-2\sqrt{3}}{4}=1.919\ldots$)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Use calculus to find the minimum value of $P$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) and (d) can be marked together.
M1: Either $\mu x\to \mu$ or $\frac{100}{x}\to \frac{\pm\lambda}{x^2}$.
A1: $\frac{dP}{dx}=-100x^{-2}+\frac{\pi+8-2\sqrt{3}}{4}$. Correct differentiation (need not be simplified). Allow $-100x^{-2}+(\text{awrt }1.919)$.
M1: Their $P'=0$ and attempt to solve as far as $x=\ldots$ (ignore poor manipulation): $-100x^{-2}+\frac{\pi+8-2\sqrt{3}}{4}=0\Rightarrow x=\ldots$
A1: $\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{\frac{400}{\pi+8-2\sqrt{3}}}$ or awrt 7.2 and no other values: $x=7.2180574\ldots$
A1: $\{x=7.218\ldots\}\Rightarrow P=27.708\ldots$(m), awrt 27.7.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Justify, by further differentiation, that the value of $P$ that you have found is a minimum.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Finds $P''$ ($x^n\to x^{n-1}$ allow for constant $\to 0$) and considers sign.
A1ft: $\frac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\frac{200}{x^3}$ (need not be simplified) and $>0\Rightarrow$ Minimum. Only follow through on a correct $P''$ and a single positive value of $x$ found earlier.

(2)

parts.mark_scheme:

M1: $(x\pm\alpha)^2+(y\pm\beta)^2=k^2$ where $A(\alpha,\beta)$ and $k$ is their radius: $(x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=225$ (or $(15)^2$).
A1: $(x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=225$. Allow $(x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=15^2$. Accept correct answer only.
Alternative using $x^2+2ax+y^2+2by+c=0$: M1: Uses $A(\pm\alpha,\pm\beta)$ and $x^2+2ax+y^2+2by+c=0$ e.g. $x^2+2(-3)x+y^2+2(1)y+c=0$. M1: Uses P or Q and $x^2+2ax+y^2+2by+c=0$ e.g. $(-9)^2+2(-3)(-9)+(8)^2+2(1)(8)+c=0\Rightarrow c=-215$. A1: $x^2-6x+y^2+2y-215=0$.
